# Seedling survival regression

A binomial logistic regression relates seedling survival to scaled conspecific
density in 60 simulated quadrats.

$$s_i\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_i,p_i),\qquad
\operatorname{logit}(p_i)=\alpha+\beta x_i.$$

- `n`: number of seedlings in a quadrat.
- `suv`: number of survivors.
- `cons`: scaled conspecific density.

The independent priors for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are Normal with mean 0 and
**SD 2.5**. The model can be fitted below or analysed using a prepared result.

**Core:** read the coefficient table, sampling checks and survival curve using
the prepared result. Running the supplied analysis code is optional. For this
route, skip both fitting sections and continue at [Prepared result](#prepared-result).

**Optional:** fit a new model with brms or Stan in a prepared environment.

## Packages and data

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(posterior)
library(bayesplot)
library(here)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 14))

ndd <- read_csv(here("data", "ndd.csv"))
```

## Optional: fit the model with brms

`brms` translates the regression formula into Stan. This fits the same binomial
logit model and independent Normal(0, 2.5) coefficient priors used below.

```{r fit-brms, eval=FALSE}
library(brms)

fit_brms <- brm(
  bf(suv | trials(n) ~ cons, center = FALSE),
  data = ndd,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  prior = set_prior("normal(0, 2.5)", class = "b"),
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  seed = 42,
  chains = 4,
  cores = 1,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  refresh = 500
)
```

`trials(n)` supplies the seedling count. `cons` predicts survival on the logit
scale. The intercept is included automatically. `center=FALSE` keeps its prior
at `cons = 0`, matching the Stan model. The coefficient names in brms are
`b_Intercept` and `b_cons`.

## Optional: fit the model with Stan

The supplied file `stan/logit_reg.stan` contains:

```stan
data {
  int<lower=0> N;               // number of quadrats
  array[N] int<lower=0> n;      // seedlings per quadrat
  array[N] int<lower=0> suv;    // survivors per quadrat
  vector[N] cons;               // conspecific density (scaled)
}

parameters {
  real alpha;                   // intercept (logit scale)
  real beta;                    // slope (logit scale)
}

model {
  // likelihood: logit(p) = alpha + beta * cons
  suv ~ binomial_logit(n, alpha + beta * cons);
  // priors
  alpha ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  beta ~ normal(0, 2.5);
}
```

The R data list connects the CSV columns to Stan's data block. `cmdstan_model()`
compiles the model, and `$sample()` runs the chains.

```{r fit-stan, eval=FALSE}
library(cmdstanr)

stan_data <- list(
  N = nrow(ndd),
  n = as.integer(ndd$n),
  suv = as.integer(ndd$suv),
  cons = ndd$cons
)

model_stan <- cmdstan_model(here("stan", "logit_reg.stan"))
fit_stan <- model_stan$sample(
  data = stan_data,
  seed = 42,
  chains = 4,
  parallel_chains = 1,
  iter_warmup = 1000,
  iter_sampling = 1000,
  refresh = 500
)
```

Both fitting sections run new inference in a prepared environment. They are
shown but not executed when this handout is rendered. Run either section to fit
the model, or skip both and use the supplied result. Students do not need to
install CmdStan, a C++ toolchain or Docker on their own computers.

## Data and posterior draws

Run **one** of the following three chunks, then continue to Summary.
Use brms or Stan after fitting that model; use the prepared result to skip fitting.
Do not run all three: each replaces the result used below.

### brms result

```{r draws-brms, eval=FALSE}
coef_draws <- as_draws_df(fit_brms, variable = c("b_Intercept", "b_cons")) |>
  rename_variables(alpha = "b_Intercept", beta = "b_cons")

sampler_diagnostics <- brms::nuts_params(fit_brms) |>
  filter(Parameter == "divergent__") |>
  summarise(num_divergent = sum(Value), .by = Chain) |>
  select(num_divergent)
```

The coefficients are renamed alpha and beta to match the equations.
`nuts_params()` supplies the sampler diagnostics; here we count divergences per chain.

### Stan result

```{r draws-stan, eval=FALSE}
coef_draws <- as_draws_df(fit_stan$draws(c("alpha", "beta")))
sampler_diagnostics <- fit_stan$diagnostic_summary()
```

### Prepared result

```{r draws-precomputed}
fit <- readRDS(here("fits", "day2_ndd.rds"))
coef_draws <- subset_draws(fit$draws, variable = c("alpha", "beta"))
sampler_diagnostics <- fit$diagnostics
```

The prepared result uses the supplied, unchanged `ndd.csv`.
All three options retain chain and iteration identifiers. The diagnostics come
from the same fit as the draws. New fits can differ slightly because of Monte
Carlo variation.

## Summary

`summarise_draws()` produces the coefficient table. The requested 2.5th and
97.5th percentiles give a **95% credible interval**.

```{r coefficient-table}
coefficient_table <- posterior::summarise_draws(
  coef_draws,
  mean = mean,
  sd = sd,
  \(x) quantile(x, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
)
coefficient_table
```

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `variable` | `alpha`: intercept; `beta`: density coefficient. |
| `mean` | Posterior mean of the coefficient. |
| `sd` | Posterior standard deviation: uncertainty about the coefficient. |
| `2.5%`, `97.5%` | Lower and upper ends of the 95% credible interval. |

$\alpha$ is log-odds at `cons = 0`. $\beta$ is the change in log-odds per
one SD increase in density. Neither coefficient is itself a probability.

In the prepared result, `beta` is negative and its credible interval excludes zero: higher density
is associated with lower survival probability under this model. This is an
association in simulated data, not evidence of a causal mechanism. Check the
sampling before using the estimates.

## Sampling diagnostics

```{r sampling-diagnostics}
sampling_table <- posterior::summarise_draws(
  coef_draws,
  rhat = posterior::rhat,
  ess_bulk = posterior::ess_bulk,
  ess_tail = posterior::ess_tail
)
sampling_table

# One row per chain, recorded when the model was fitted.
sampler_table <- as_tibble(sampler_diagnostics) |>
  mutate(chain = row_number(), .before = 1)
sampler_table
```

- **`rhat`:** compares chains. Values near 1 are encouraging; values above 1.01
  are a reason to investigate.
- **`ess_bulk`, `ess_tail`:** effective sample sizes for central values and tails
  of the posterior. They account for dependence among draws and are not seedling
  sample sizes. For these four chains, values below about 400 warrant investigation.
- **`num_divergent`:** divergent transitions after warmup, recorded for each chain.
  Investigate any nonzero count.

Stan and prepared results also show `num_max_treedepth` and `ebfmi`, additional
sampler checks that the instructor can explain.

The prepared CNDD result has R-hat near 1, bulk/tail ESS above 400 and zero
divergences. For a new fit, inspect the numbers produced by that fit. These are encouraging checks, not proof of convergence or sufficient
precision for every use. The trace plots provide a complementary view.

## Trace plots

```{r trace-plots}
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(coef_draws, pars = c("alpha", "beta"))
```

The horizontal axis is saved sampling step, the vertical axis is a coefficient,
and colours identify chains. These are post-warmup samples.

The prepared result's chains cover similar ranges without persistent separation
or drift. Interpret a new fit using its own traces and numerical diagnostics. Overlap alone
does not establish convergence; a single jump alone does not indicate failure.

## Survival probabilities

Each row of `curve_draws` combines one saved coefficient pair with one density.
`plogis(alpha + beta * cons)` converts log-odds into survival probability.
We calculate probabilities for every paired draw before summarising them.

```{r curve-probabilities}
density_grid <- tibble(
  cons = seq(min(ndd$cons), max(ndd$cons), length.out = 81)
)
curve_draws <- as_tibble(coef_draws) |>
  select(.draw, alpha, beta) |>
  crossing(density_grid) |>
  mutate(p = plogis(alpha + beta * cons))

curve_summary <- curve_draws |>
  group_by(cons) |>
  summarise(
    median = median(p),
    lower = quantile(p, 0.025),
    upper = quantile(p, 0.975),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

At each density, `median`, `lower` and `upper` summarise the posterior distribution
of survival probability. The alpha and beta from each draw stay together.

## Regression plot

```{r regression-plot}
regression_plot <- ggplot(curve_summary, aes(x = cons)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = "#d95f02", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median), colour = "#d95f02", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = ndd, aes(y = suv / n), alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Conspecific density (scaled)", y = "Survival probability")
regression_plot
```

- **Line:** posterior median of survival probability.
- **Ribbon:** 95% credible interval for survival probability at each density.
- **Points:** observed survivor proportions, one per quadrat.

For the prepared result, the fitted curve decreases with density, consistent
with the negative coefficient.
The ribbon describes uncertainty about probability; it need not contain every
observed proportion. Observed proportions also vary because survival is binomial.

The `alpha` argument in `geom_ribbon()` controls transparency; it is unrelated
to the regression intercept $\alpha$.

Sampling diagnostics tell us about computation; they do not establish that the
ecological model is appropriate.

[The result sheet](results.html) provides the same outputs without the code.

# Instructor reference

Follow the code and outputs in order: summary, diagnostics, traces, probability
calculation and plotting. This is a guided walkthrough, not a worksheet with
separate questions, written answers or timed tasks. Explain the coefficient
rows and table columns directly, then connect beta's sign to the curve.

The coefficient mean is not MLE or MAP, and posterior SD is not Monte Carlo
standard error. The plot uses a posterior median; neither summary needs to
represent one sampled coefficient pair. Its credible intervals are pointwise,
not a simultaneous interval for the entire curve or a predictive interval for
survivor counts. Do not summarise alpha and beta separately before transforming.

The root exercise uses CmdStan `$summary()` and brms `summary()`. Our stored file
is a list of posterior draws and diagnostics, so `summarise_draws()` supplies
the corresponding coefficient table. `summary(fit)` would describe the list.
The prepared result corresponds to the supplied CSV and Stan model. If either
is changed, fit the changed model rather than reusing the prepared result.

Also check parameter-level diagnostics including `lp__`, treedepth, E-BFMI and
Monte Carlo precision for the intended quantities. Do not copy the root file's
automatic good/bad classifications or its E-BFMI quality scale. Computation and
ecological model appropriateness are different issues. The lecture includes one
existing PPC figure; predictive simulation details remain optional reference.

## Choosing the fitting route

Use either live fitting section when the prepared environment and class pace
permit. Run just one of the three result-loading chunks. Only the prepared
result is executed when rendering the handout; live-result chunks have
`eval=FALSE`. Do not use stored diagnostics to validate a new fit.

The brms formula uses `bf(suv | trials(n) ~ cons, center=FALSE)` so both
coefficient priors match `stan/logit_reg.stan`. Disabling internal centering
keeps the intercept prior at cons=0; a plain `~ cons` would instead apply the
intercept prior at the sample mean of cons. The brms result-loading chunk shows
only divergence counts. Check treedepth, E-BFMI and other sampler details using
the complete `nuts_params(fit_brms)` output when needed. In normal-prior R/Stan syntax, 2.5 is an SD. Rendering
never compiles or samples the two fitting sections. No local student toolchain
installation is required; validate any classroom live-fitting environment ahead
of class. Compilation time and simultaneous server load are separate concerns.

References: [brms formulas](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/brmsformula.html),
[brms draws](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/draws-brms.html),
[posterior summaries](https://mc-stan.org/posterior/reference/draws_summary.html)
and [Stan diagnostic guidance](https://mc-stan.org/learn-stan/diagnostics-warnings.html).
:::
